sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS1-1: Develop and use a model of the Earth-sun-moon system to describe the cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses of the sun and moon, and seasons
OpenStax Astronomy 2e, 2.1 The Sky Above (23.5° tilt)

note.text: Seasons are changes in how much heat we get from the sun through the year.

steps.title: Orbit
steps.instruction: Trace Earth's orbit, seen at a slant from the side.

note.text: Earth's distance from the sun changes by only about 3%. That's too little to cause the seasons.

steps.title: Earth in June
steps.instruction: Trace Earth on the right of the sun.

note.text: This is Earth in June. Six months later it's on the far side of its orbit.

steps.title: Axis and equator
steps.instruction: Draw the tilted axis through the poles, then the equator.

note.text: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. In June, the north end leans toward the sun.

steps.title: Earth in December
steps.instruction: Trace Earth on the left of the sun.

note.text: This is Earth in December, halfway around its orbit.

steps.title: Same tilt
steps.instruction: Draw the axis and equator, tilted the same way as before.

note.text: The axis keeps pointing the same direction in space all year. Now the north end leans away from the sun.

steps.title: Sunlight
steps.instruction: Draw the two arrows of sunlight.

note.text: The half leaning toward the sun gets more direct light and longer days, so it heats up more.

steps.title: Which season?
steps.instruction: Pick the season in the Northern Hemisphere for each Earth.

targets.role: North end leans toward the sun.

mistakes.Winter: The north end leans toward the sun here, so the north gets direct light and long days: summer.

targets.role: North end leans away from the sun.

mistakes.Summer: Here the north leans away, so its sunlight is spread out and days are short: winter.

options.text: The tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the sun
options.feedback: Yes. Through the year, each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the sun, getting more direct light.

options.text: Earth getting closer to the sun in summer
options.feedback: Earth is actually closest to the sun in January, during northern winter.

options.text: The sun getting hotter in summer
options.feedback: The sun's output barely changes. The tilt changes how directly its light hits us.
Earth's spin gives day and night, not seasons. The tilt causes the seasons.

steps.title: Other hemisphere
steps.question: It's June. What season is it in Australia, in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.feedback: Right. In June the south end leans away from the sun, so the seasons are opposite.
If distance caused the seasons, both halves would match. They're opposite, because of the tilt.
Spring and autumn come when Earth leans neither toward nor away, in March and September.
The Southern Hemisphere has seasons too, just opposite to the north's.
